question: Under RELRA Section 604(a)(12), from whom may a licensed salesperson or associate broker accept a commission or other valuable consideration for performing a licensed real estate act?
choice_a: Only from the licensed real estate broker with whom the salesperson or associate broker is affiliated
choice_b: From any party to the transaction who offers to pay, as long as it is disclosed afterward
choice_c: From any licensed broker in the state, whether or not the salesperson is affiliated with that broker
choice_d: From the consumer directly, so long as the broker consents in writing
explanation: RELRA Section 604(a)(12) makes it a prohibited act for a salesperson or associate broker to accept a commission or other valuable consideration for licensed acts from any person other than the licensed broker with whom he or she is affiliated -- compensation for licensed activity must flow through the affiliated broker.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.604(a)(12) (confirmed verbatim)

question: A title insurance agency offers a PA-licensed salesperson a $200 cash 'thank you' directly for every closing referred to it, paid straight to the salesperson rather than routed through the salesperson's broker. Under RELRA Section 604(a)(12), is this permissible?
choice_a: No -- a salesperson may not accept compensation for a licensed real estate act from anyone other than the broker with whom the salesperson is affiliated
choice_b: Yes, as long as the salesperson reports the payment on a personal tax return
choice_c: Yes, because title agencies are exempt from RELRA's compensation restrictions
choice_d: Yes, provided the amount is under $250
explanation: Section 604(a)(12) squarely bars a salesperson from taking outside compensation tied to a licensed act from anyone but the affiliated broker; a referral payment routed directly to the salesperson bypasses that requirement regardless of amount, and would also raise separate RESPA concerns.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.604(a)(12) (confirmed verbatim)

question: Under RELRA Section 604(a)(12.1), to whom may a broker pay a commission or other valuable consideration for the performance of a licensed real estate act?
choice_a: Only to the broker's own licensed employees or to another real estate broker
choice_b: To anyone the broker chooses, licensed or not, as long as a 1099 is issued
choice_c: To any relative of the broker regardless of licensure
choice_d: To any person who signed a referral agreement, licensed or not
explanation: Section 604(a)(12.1) is the broker-side mirror of Section 604(a)(12): a broker may pay a commission or other valuable consideration for licensed acts only to the broker's own licensed employees or to another real estate broker -- paying an unlicensed person for performing licensed activity is prohibited regardless of documentation.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.604(a)(12.1) (confirmed verbatim)

question: A broker's unlicensed neighbor mentions to a friend that a house is for sale, the friend ends up buying it through the broker, and the broker pays the neighbor a $500 'finder's fee' for the tip. Does this violate RELRA?
choice_a: Yes -- Section 604(a)(12.1) prohibits a broker from paying a commission or other valuable consideration to anyone other than the broker's licensed employees or another real estate broker
choice_b: No, because the neighbor never negotiated any contract terms
choice_c: No, because finder's fees under $1,000 are exempt from RELRA
choice_d: No, because only the buyer's consent is required, not licensure
explanation: Merely giving a tip does not require a license, but PAYING that unlicensed tipster a fee tied to the resulting transaction is exactly what Section 604(a)(12.1) forbids -- the statute bars the broker from compensating anyone but licensed employees or another broker for performance connected to licensed acts, with no dollar-amount exception.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.604(a)(12.1) (confirmed verbatim)

question: RELRA Section 604(a)(12.1) permits a broker to pay a commission to 'another real estate broker.' Does this cover a referral fee paid to a broker licensed only in a different state?
choice_a: The exception's plain text is not limited to Pennsylvania-licensed brokers, so a referral fee to a broker licensed and acting as a broker in another jurisdiction falls within the 'another real estate broker' exception
choice_b: No -- only brokers holding an active Pennsylvania license may ever receive a referral fee from a Pennsylvania broker
choice_c: Interstate referral fees between brokers are always illegal under federal law
choice_d: The exception applies only to brokers who are members of the same MLS
explanation: Unlike the salesperson-to-broker limitation in 604(a)(12), the 604(a)(12.1) exception simply says 'another real estate broker' without restricting it to Pennsylvania licensees, which is why broker-to-broker referral arrangements across state lines are common industry practice; the key restriction the statute enforces is that the RECIPIENT must be a licensed broker (or the paying broker's own licensed employee), not an unlicensed party.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.604(a)(12.1) (confirmed verbatim); interstate-referral industry practice is well-corroborated but not itself independently pinpoint-cited to a specific RELRA cross-jurisdiction provision in this research pass

question: Under RELRA Section 604(a)(11), what makes it a prohibited act to induce a party to break an existing contract?
choice_a: Inducing a party to break a contract in order to substitute a new contract, where the substitution is motivated by the licensee's own personal gain
choice_b: Any communication at all with a party who is already under contract with another licensee
choice_c: Advising a client that a contract may be voidable under general contract law
choice_d: Recommending that a client consult an attorney before signing a new listing
explanation: Section 604(a)(11) is narrowly aimed at self-interested contract interference: it prohibits inducing a party to break a contract for the purpose of substituting a new one, specifically where that substitution is motivated by the licensee's personal gain -- a classic scenario being a licensee talking a seller out of an existing listing to grab the commission on a replacement listing.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.604(a)(11) (confirmed verbatim)

question: Under RELRA Section 604(a)(13), what must a licensee disclose in writing to an owner before purchasing, or acquiring any interest or option in, property listed with the licensee's own office?
choice_a: The licensee's intention or true position -- that the licensee is, directly or indirectly through a third party, acquiring an interest in the listed property
choice_b: Nothing -- licensees are categorically barred from ever purchasing listed property
choice_c: Only the purchase price, not the fact that the licensee is the buyer
choice_d: The disclosure is required only if the purchase price exceeds the listing price
explanation: Section 604(a)(13) does not ban a licensee from buying listed property, but it does require the licensee to disclose in writing his or her true position -- that the licensee is directly or indirectly (even through a third party) purchasing, acquiring an interest in, or acquiring an option on the very property listed with the licensee's office -- a self-dealing disclosure closely tied to the licensee's compensation incentive as listing agent.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.604(a)(13) (confirmed verbatim)

question: What does RELRA Section 604(a)(19) prohibit with respect to commissions, rebates, and other compensation?
choice_a: Paying or accepting, giving or charging, any undisclosed commission, rebate, compensation, or profit, or expenditures for a principal, in violation of the act
choice_b: Charging any commission at all above 6% of the sale price
choice_c: Disclosing any commission arrangement to a principal without the Commission's prior written approval
choice_d: Paying a commission split to an affiliated salesperson under any circumstances
explanation: Section 604(a)(19) is a broad catch-all: it makes it a prohibited act to pay, accept, give, or charge any UNDISCLOSED commission, rebate, compensation, or profit (or expenditure made for a principal) in violation of the act -- the core problem being secrecy, not the existence of a commission or rebate itself.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.604(a)(19) (confirmed verbatim)

question: A buyer's agent offers to rebate part of the agent's commission to the buyer at closing to help with costs, but never tells the seller or the seller's agent about the rebate. Does RELRA Section 604(a)(19) permit this?
choice_a: No -- Section 604(a)(19) prohibits giving any UNDISCLOSED commission, rebate, or compensation; the rebate itself is not illegal, but concealing it is
choice_b: Yes, because commission rebates to buyers are always illegal in Pennsylvania regardless of disclosure
choice_c: Yes, because only rebates to sellers require disclosure
choice_d: No, because RELRA bans all commission rebates to consumers outright
explanation: Section 604(a)(19)'s language targets the failure to disclose, not the underlying practice of rebating -- a properly disclosed buyer-agent rebate is a routine, permissible practice in many transactions, but the same rebate given quietly, without disclosure to the other parties to the transaction, falls within the statute's prohibition.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.604(a)(19) (confirmed verbatim)

question: Under RELRA Section 604(a)(10), what must every listing agreement specify regarding its duration?
choice_a: A definite termination date
choice_b: No termination date is required as long as the fee is disclosed
choice_c: A minimum term of one year
choice_d: An automatic renewal clause is mandatory
explanation: Section 604(a)(10) makes it a prohibited act to fail to specify a definite termination date in a listing agreement -- an open-ended listing with no fixed end date leaves both the consumer's exit rights and the broker's commission entitlement unclear, which is exactly what this provision is designed to prevent.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.604(a)(10) (confirmed verbatim)

question: Under RELRA Section 604(a)(9), what must a licensee do regarding copies of a contract, such as a listing or compensation agreement, that a consumer has signed?
choice_a: Furnish a copy of the contract to every party who signed it
choice_b: Retain the only copy in the broker's file and provide it to the consumer only on request
choice_c: Provide a copy only if the consumer pays a reproduction fee
choice_d: Provide a copy only after closing
explanation: Section 604(a)(9) makes it a prohibited act to fail to furnish a copy of any contract -- including a listing or compensation agreement -- to each party who signed it, at the time of signing, so that every signatory has the actual document memorializing the negotiated fee and other terms.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.604(a)(9) (confirmed verbatim)

question: Under RELRA Section 201's definitions, does the term 'employ' (and related terms like 'employee' and 'employment') apply only to a traditional employer-employee relationship between a broker and salesperson?
choice_a: No -- RELRA Section 201 provides that 'employ,' 'employed,' 'employee,' and 'employment' apply to the relationship of independent contractor as well as to the relationship of employment, with an exception for builder-owner salespersons
choice_b: Yes -- RELRA recognizes only W-2 employment between brokers and salespersons
choice_c: Yes -- independent contractor salespersons are entirely outside RELRA's supervisory scheme
choice_d: The terms have no defined meaning under RELRA and are governed solely by the IRS
explanation: Because most Pennsylvania salespersons are compensated as independent contractors for tax purposes, RELRA Section 201 makes clear that 'employ,' 'employed,' 'employee,' and 'employment' extend to the independent contractor relationship as well as to conventional employment -- ensuring a broker's licensing-law supervisory duties over an affiliated salesperson do not evaporate simply because the salesperson is paid on a 1099 rather than a W-2 basis.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.201 (confirmed, definitions section); consistent with codes.findlaw.com's published text of Section 455.201

question: RELRA Section 201's rule that 'employment' includes independent contractor relationships carries one named exception. Which category of salesperson is excepted?
choice_a: A builder-owner salesperson
choice_b: A cemetery salesperson
choice_c: A time-share salesperson
choice_d: There is no exception -- the rule applies universally
explanation: RELRA Section 201 extends the 'employ'/'employee'/'employment' definitions to independent contractor arrangements generally, but expressly carves out builder-owner salespersons from that extension, reflecting the distinct, narrower licensing category builder-owner salespersons occupy under the act.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.201 (confirmed, definitions section)

question: A broker properly classifies an affiliated salesperson as an independent contractor for federal tax purposes. Does this independent contractor status relieve the broker of RELRA's supervisory responsibility over that salesperson's licensed activity?
choice_a: No -- because RELRA Section 201 treats the independent contractor relationship the same as employment for purposes of the act, the broker's duty to supervise the salesperson's licensed conduct is unaffected by the salesperson's tax classification
choice_b: Yes -- independent contractors are entirely self-supervising under Pennsylvania law
choice_c: Yes -- only W-2 salespersons are subject to broker supervision requirements
choice_d: The question is unsettled and has never been addressed by RELRA or its regulations
explanation: Tax classification and licensing-law supervisory duty are separate legal questions: a salesperson's independent-contractor status for IRS purposes governs employment tax withholding, not the broker's RELRA obligation to supervise the licensed activity of everyone affiliated with the broker, which Section 201's inclusive definition of 'employment' is written to preserve.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.201 (confirmed definitional inclusion of independent contractor relationships); broker supervisory-duty framework cross-referenced against RELRA Sections 604(a)(16) and 701-702 (confirmed from this bank's other broker-supervision buckets)

question: Under federal tax law (26 U.S.C. Section 3508), what three conditions must be met for a real estate salesperson to be treated as a 'qualified real estate agent' -- i.e., NOT an employee for federal tax purposes?
choice_a: The individual must be a licensed real estate agent; substantially all of the individual's compensation must be directly related to sales output rather than hours worked; and the services must be performed under a written contract stating the individual will not be treated as an employee for federal tax purposes
choice_b: The individual must work at least 40 hours per week, be paid hourly, and have a written W-2 agreement
choice_c: The individual must hold a broker's license, work fewer than 20 hours per week, and waive all workers' compensation coverage
choice_d: The individual must be affiliated with only one broker for at least five consecutive years
explanation: 26 U.S.C. Section 3508(b)(1) defines a 'qualified real estate agent' using a three-part test: (A) the individual is a licensed real estate agent, (B) substantially all compensation is tied to sales or other output rather than hours worked, and (C) the services are performed under a written contract providing that the individual will not be treated as an employee for federal tax purposes -- meeting all three keeps a commission-only salesperson off payroll taxes and out of employee status federally.
source_note: 26 U.S.C. Section 3508(b)(1) (confirmed verbatim via uscode.house.gov, Office of the Law Revision Counsel); hedge: standard federal tax law, not a Pennsylvania-specific provision, consistent with this bank's convention for national/federal doctrine

question: A broker pays an affiliated salesperson strictly on commission but never signs a written contract stating the salesperson will not be treated as an employee for federal tax purposes. Under 26 U.S.C. Section 3508, what is the consequence?
choice_a: The salesperson fails the 'qualified real estate agent' test because the written-contract element is missing, exposing the arrangement to reclassification as a conventional employment relationship for federal tax purposes
choice_b: Nothing -- only the commission-based-pay element matters under Section 3508
choice_c: The broker automatically loses their real estate license
choice_d: The salesperson is automatically deemed an independent contractor regardless of the missing writing
explanation: All three prongs of 26 U.S.C. Section 3508(b)(1) -- licensure, output-based pay, and a written non-employee contract -- must be satisfied together; omitting the written contract element means the safe harbor is not met, which is why brokerages routinely require a signed independent contractor agreement as a condition of commission-only affiliation.
source_note: 26 U.S.C. Section 3508(b)(1) (confirmed verbatim via uscode.house.gov); hedge: standard federal tax law, not Pennsylvania-specific

question: Consistent with commission-only, independent-contractor-style compensation, how does a broker typically report a salesperson's annual commission income to the IRS?
choice_a: On Form 1099-NEC, rather than a Form W-2, because the compensation is not wages subject to payroll withholding
choice_b: On Form W-2 only, identical to hourly staff
choice_c: No federal reporting is required for real estate commission income
choice_d: On Form 1099-DIV, since commissions are treated as investment income
explanation: Because a properly structured broker-salesperson relationship treats the salesperson as an independent contractor for tax purposes (see 26 U.S.C. Section 3508), commission income is reported on Form 1099-NEC rather than withheld and reported on a W-2 -- a practical consequence of the independent contractor classification that candidates are expected to understand.
source_note: hedge: standard federal tax-reporting practice for independent contractor real estate agents, consistent with 26 U.S.C. Section 3508's qualified-real-estate-agent framework; not independently pinpoint-cited to an IRS form instruction in this research pass

question: Under federal antitrust law (the Sherman Antitrust Act), may competing real estate brokers in the same market agree among themselves to charge a uniform commission rate?
choice_a: No -- horizontal agreements among competing brokers to fix commission rates are illegal price-fixing under the Sherman Antitrust Act, regardless of what any state licensing law says about negotiability
choice_b: Yes, as long as the local Board of REALTORS approves the rate
choice_c: Yes, as long as the agreed rate is published publicly in advance
choice_d: Yes, but only for commercial (not residential) transactions
explanation: Commission-rate collusion among competing brokerages is horizontal price fixing, a per se violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act -- this is precisely why RELRA and its state-law counterparts require disclosures that fees are the product of negotiation rather than a fixed schedule, and why the Real Estate Commission does not (and could not) set or approve a uniform commission rate.
source_note: hedge: standard federal antitrust doctrine (Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. Section 1, per se horizontal price-fixing rule as applied to real estate commissions), well-established and industry-standard rather than a Pennsylvania-specific provision

question: Under the 'procuring cause' doctrine tested on the national broker outline, which broker is generally entitled to a commission when more than one broker had contact with the eventual buyer?
choice_a: The broker whose uninterrupted chain of events was the predominating, effective cause in bringing about the sale
choice_b: Whichever broker's name appears first alphabetically on the listing paperwork
choice_c: The broker who spent the most total advertising dollars on the property
choice_d: Only the listing broker, regardless of who actually introduced the buyer
explanation: Procuring cause looks at which broker's efforts formed the uninterrupted chain of events that was the predominating, effective cause of the buyer and seller coming to terms -- a fact-specific inquiry frequently at the center of commission disputes between cooperating brokers, and a standard national-exam topic tested independently of any single state's licensing statute.
source_note: Pearson VUE National/General Exam Content Outline for Brokers, effective April 1, 2025, listing/commission topics (confirmed general subject matter); hedge: standard national real estate doctrine, not a Pennsylvania-specific statutory provision

question: Under the 'ready, willing, and able buyer' doctrine, when has a broker generally earned a commission on an exclusive right-to-sell listing?
choice_a: Once the broker procures a buyer who is ready, willing, and financially able to purchase on the seller's terms -- even if the seller later refuses to complete the sale
choice_b: Only once the deed has actually been recorded
choice_c: Only once the buyer's mortgage has fully closed and funded
choice_d: Never, unless the seller voluntarily pays regardless of any legal entitlement
explanation: The ready-willing-and-able-buyer doctrine holds that a broker has fully performed, and is generally entitled to the commission, once the broker produces a buyer who is ready, willing, and financially able to buy on the seller's stated terms -- meaning a seller's own later refusal to close does not automatically extinguish the broker's earned commission, distinguishing 'earning' the commission from actually collecting it.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate commission-law doctrine tested on the Pearson VUE National/General Exam Content Outline for Brokers, effective April 1, 2025; not a Pennsylvania-specific statutory citation

question: What is the purpose of a 'safety clause' (also called a protection or extension clause) in an exclusive listing agreement?
choice_a: It protects the broker's commission if a buyer the broker procured and introduced during the listing term ultimately purchases the property shortly after the listing expires
choice_b: It guarantees the seller a minimum sale price regardless of market conditions
choice_c: It automatically extends every listing indefinitely until the property sells
choice_d: It shields the seller from ever having to pay any commission after the listing expires
explanation: A safety (protection/extension) clause addresses the risk that a seller waits out the listing term with a broker-introduced buyer, then closes just after expiration to avoid the commission; the clause preserves the broker's commission entitlement for a defined post-expiration window as to buyers the broker actually procured and identified during the listing period -- standard national listing-agreement content.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate listing-agreement doctrine, industry-standard and tested on the national exam outline rather than tied to a specific RELRA section

question: When two cooperating brokers (e.g., a listing broker and a buyer's broker) dispute which one is entitled to a commission on a completed sale, where is that dispute typically resolved?
choice_a: Through mandatory arbitration under NAR's Code of Ethics (Article 17) if both brokers are REALTOR members of the same association, rather than before the Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission
choice_b: Exclusively before the Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission, which adjudicates all commission disputes statewide
choice_c: Automatically in favor of whichever broker filed first with the county recorder of deeds
choice_d: Commission disputes between cooperating brokers cannot be resolved by any process
explanation: The Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission's disciplinary jurisdiction addresses violations of RELRA and its regulations, not garden-variety fee splits between cooperating brokers; where both brokers are REALTOR association members, Article 17 of the NAR Code of Ethics requires mandatory arbitration of such commission disputes through the local association rather than through the state licensing agency or (typically) the courts.
source_note: hedge: standard national practice under the NAR Code of Ethics, Article 17 (mandatory arbitration of commission disputes among REALTOR members); not a Pennsylvania statutory provision

question: The federal Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA), Section 8, prohibits what kind of arrangement involving referrals of settlement service business (such as title insurance or mortgage services)?
choice_a: Kickbacks or unearned referral fees paid or received in exchange for the referral of settlement service business
choice_b: Any advertising of settlement services whatsoever
choice_c: Referring a client to any title company at all, under any circumstances
choice_d: Charging any fee for title insurance
explanation: RESPA Section 8 (12 U.S.C. Section 2607) prohibits giving or accepting a fee, kickback, or thing of value in exchange for referring settlement service business -- a federal anti-kickback rule distinct from, but conceptually related to, RELRA's own restrictions on undisclosed compensation and payments to unlicensed persons for licensed real estate acts.
source_note: hedge: standard federal law (RESPA Section 8, 12 U.S.C. Section 2607), well-established and industry-standard rather than Pennsylvania-specific; consistent with this bank's treatment of other federal RESPA/TILA content per the pa_re_broker.json handbookNote

question: Effective August 17, 2024, following the National Association of REALTORS' nationwide settlement, what changed about how broker compensation may be communicated on an MLS?
choice_a: MLS Participants and sellers may no longer include any offer of compensation to a buyer's broker on the MLS itself -- compensation offers were removed from MLS listing data entirely
choice_b: Nothing changed -- MLS compensation fields remain mandatory nationwide
choice_c: MLS compensation offers became mandatory for every listing, replacing optional disclosure
choice_d: The settlement only affected commercial MLS listings, not residential ones
explanation: As part of the NAR settlement, MLS policy effective August 17, 2024 eliminated and prohibited offers of buyer-broker compensation being placed in the MLS by sellers or listing participants, including in remarks or other free-text fields -- compensation to a buyer's broker can still be negotiated, but no longer through the MLS listing itself.
source_note: hedge: standard national industry development, well-corroborated via NAR's own published settlement FAQ and MLS policy summary; not a Pennsylvania-specific RELRA provision but broadly applicable to PA-licensed brokers using MLS systems

question: Following the same 2024 NAR settlement-driven MLS policy changes, what must a buyer's agent generally have in place with a buyer before touring homes with that buyer?
choice_a: A written buyer representation agreement
choice_b: Nothing -- no agreement of any kind is required before touring homes
choice_c: A verbal agreement is sufficient and a writing is expressly disallowed
choice_d: Written approval from the listing broker of every home to be toured
explanation: The settlement-driven MLS Participant rule requires real estate professionals using an MLS to enter into a written buyer agreement with a buyer before touring a home with that buyer -- a national practice change that also reinforces RELRA's own longstanding preference for written buyer-agency agreements (see Section 608.1(5) and the narrow oral-agreement exception in Section 606.1(b)(2)).
source_note: hedge: standard national industry development, well-corroborated via NAR's own published settlement FAQ; cross-referenced against 63 P.S. Section 455.606.1(b)(2) (confirmed verbatim, from this bucket's earlier content) for the PA written-agreement context

question: After the 2024 NAR settlement removed compensation offers from the MLS, may a seller still agree to pay or contribute toward a buyer's broker's compensation?
choice_a: Yes -- seller concessions toward buyer-broker compensation remain permissible, but must now be negotiated directly between the parties rather than advertised as an MLS compensation offer
choice_b: No -- sellers are now categorically barred from ever contributing to buyer-broker compensation
choice_c: Yes, but only if the amount is disclosed in the MLS remarks field
choice_d: Only if the buyer's broker is unaffiliated with any brokerage
explanation: The settlement changed WHERE and HOW buyer-broker compensation may be communicated -- removing it from the MLS -- but did not ban seller concessions toward that compensation; such arrangements are still negotiated off-MLS, typically within the purchase agreement itself, consistent with RELRA's own emphasis (Section 608.1(1)) that all such fees remain the product of negotiation.
source_note: hedge: standard national industry development, well-corroborated via NAR's own published settlement FAQ; cross-referenced against 63 P.S. Section 455.608.1(1) (confirmed verbatim, from this bucket's earlier content)

question: RELRA Section 608.3(a) requires a comparative market analysis (CMA) to conspicuously disclose it was not prepared under USPAP and is not an appraisal. Under RELRA Section 608.6, does a similar disclosure apply to a broker price opinion (BPO)?
choice_a: Yes -- Section 608.6 imposes parallel disclosure language for broker price opinions, requiring that a BPO likewise be conspicuously identified as not prepared under USPAP and not to be used as an appraisal
choice_b: No -- broker price opinions are entirely unregulated under RELRA
choice_c: No -- only CMAs require any disclosure; BPOs may be presented as formal appraisals
choice_d: Yes, but only for BPOs prepared on commercial property
explanation: RELRA Section 608.6 extends the same USPAP/not-an-appraisal disclosure concept from CMAs (Section 608.3(a)) to broker price opinions, since both products can be mistaken for a formal appraisal if not clearly labeled -- consumer protection against a licensee's informal valuation being relied upon as if it carried appraisal-level rigor.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.608.6 (confirmed general subject matter, parallel to Section 608.3(a) per this project's earlier verbatim confirmation, noted in pa_re_broker.json's handbookNote); precise subsection lettering of 608.6 not independently re-verified word-for-word in this research pass

question: Parallel to RELRA Section 608.3(c)'s rule for comparative market analyses, who is entitled to keep a fee charged for a broker price opinion under Section 608.6?
choice_a: The fee shall be paid to the broker, consistent with the same broker-of-record compensation principle that governs CMA fees
choice_b: The fee belongs personally to the salesperson who physically prepared the opinion
choice_c: The fee must be forwarded to the client requesting the opinion
choice_d: Broker price opinions may never be charged for under Pennsylvania law
explanation: Just as Section 608.3(c) directs CMA fees to the broker rather than the individual preparing salesperson, Section 608.6's parallel structure for broker price opinions follows the same principle -- compensation for licensed valuation-adjacent work flows through the broker, consistent with RELRA Section 604(a)(12)'s broader rule that salespersons may not personally retain outside compensation for licensed acts.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.608.6 (confirmed general subject matter, parallel to Section 608.3(c) per this project's earlier verbatim confirmation, noted in pa_re_broker.json's handbookNote); precise subsection lettering of 608.6 not independently re-verified word-for-word in this research pass

question: While RELRA requires that fees charged to consumers result from negotiation (Section 608.1(1)), what governs the internal commission split between a broker and an affiliated salesperson on a given transaction?
choice_a: The broker's and salesperson's own private employment or independent-contractor agreement, which RELRA does not dictate
choice_b: A statewide split schedule published annually by the Real Estate Commission
choice_c: Whatever split the buyer's agent unilaterally selects
choice_d: A fixed 50/50 split mandated by RELRA Section 604
explanation: RELRA governs the broker's compensation relationship with the CONSUMER (through Sections 606.1(b) and 608.1) but leaves the INTERNAL split between a broker and an affiliated salesperson to their own private employment or independent-contractor agreement -- there is no statutory schedule, minimum, or mandated ratio for that internal arrangement.
source_note: 63 P.S. Sections 455.608.1(1) and 455.606.1(b)(1) (confirmed verbatim, from this bucket's earlier content); absence of any RELRA-mandated broker-salesperson split ratio confirmed via full-text review of the Act's Chapter 6 (Sections 601-610)

question: When a salesperson terminates affiliation with a broker while a transaction the salesperson worked on is still pending, who is generally entitled to any resulting commission?
choice_a: Whatever the terms of the broker-salesperson employment/independent-contractor agreement provide -- RELRA does not automatically forfeit or automatically vest pending-transaction commissions upon a salesperson's departure
choice_b: The commission is automatically forfeited to the Real Estate Recovery Fund
choice_c: The departing salesperson is automatically entitled to the full commission regardless of any agreement
choice_d: The new broker the salesperson joins automatically inherits the commission
explanation: Because commission splits and entitlement upon departure are matters of private contract between broker and salesperson rather than RELRA-mandated outcomes, what happens to a pending commission when a salesperson leaves mid-transaction depends entirely on the terms the broker and salesperson agreed to -- brokerages commonly address this scenario explicitly in their independent-contractor agreements.
source_note: hedge: standard industry practice regarding broker-salesperson independent-contractor agreements; RELRA itself does not address post-departure commission entitlement, confirmed via full-text review of the Act's Chapter 6 (Sections 601-610)

question: Because RELRA Section 606.1(b)(1) permits only a broker (not an individual salesperson) to be the counterparty to a written fee agreement with a consumer, what does this imply about who legally 'owns' a listing and its underlying compensation agreement?
choice_a: The listing and its compensation agreement belong to the broker of record, since only the broker can lawfully enter into the written agreement with the consumer under Section 606.1(b)(1)
choice_b: The listing belongs personally to whichever salesperson obtained it, independent of the broker
choice_c: Listings are jointly owned by the salesperson and the consumer
choice_d: RELRA is silent on which party holds the listing, so ownership is undefined
explanation: Because Section 606.1(b)(1) frames the enforceable written fee agreement as one 'between the broker and the consumer,' the listing and the compensation right it creates run to the broker of record -- which is also why a salesperson generally cannot take an active listing along when leaving a brokerage without the broker's consent, since the salesperson was never the actual contracting party.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.606.1(b)(1) (confirmed verbatim, from this bucket's earlier content); broker-of-record concept cross-referenced against 49 Pa. Code Section 35.201 (confirmed in pa_re_broker.json's handbookNote)

question: If a real estate office charges different commission rates for different service levels (e.g., a discounted 'limited service' listing versus a full-service listing), what does sound national practice require regarding how those different rates are presented to consumers?
choice_a: Each rate structure must be accurately and separately disclosed -- a broker may not misrepresent a variable-rate or discount structure as if it were a single fixed, non-negotiable commission
choice_b: Only the higher of the two rates may ever be disclosed to a consumer
choice_c: Variable commission structures are illegal nationwide
choice_d: No disclosure of differing rate structures is ever required
explanation: Offering tiered or discounted service levels at different commission rates is a lawful, common practice, but presenting any of those rates as fixed or non-negotiable -- rather than accurately disclosing the actual variable structure and what each tier includes -- risks misleading the consumer, contrary to the negotiated-fee transparency principle RELRA Section 608.1(1) embodies and to general consumer-protection and industry ethics standards.
source_note: hedge: standard national consumer-protection/industry-ethics principle regarding variable-rate commission disclosure, consistent with RELRA Section 608.1(1)'s negotiated-fee disclosure requirement (confirmed verbatim, from this bucket's earlier content); not itself an independently pinpoint-cited RELRA subsection
